tool.name: InvertRaster

summary.para:
View online help files: https://www.jennessent.com/corridor-designer-tools/invert-raster.html
Numerically inverts a raster -- each output cell is 1/(x + c) -- so a surface in which high values mean good habitat (a diversity index, a Land Facet Density raster) becomes a least-cost surface in which that good ground is cheap to cross. A single-band input produces one output raster; a multi-band Land Facet Density raster produces one single-band cost raster per facet, named from its own records, with the stored integer scaling converted back to 0-1 proportions first. The small constant c (default 0.1) prevents zero cells from dividing to NoData. An alternative linear method (100 - x) reproduces the ArcMap CorridorDesigner CorridorModel tool's internal suitability-to-cost conversion for 0-100 habitat suitability models. Every output records its place in the Land Facet analysis chain. A modernized port of the Land Facet Corridor Designer's Invert Raster tool. Needs no Spatial Analyst.

tool.usage:
What this tool does. Least-cost corridor tools read their input upside down from the way habitat surfaces are usually made: low cells are easy to cross and high cells are barriers. The surfaces this tool family produces measure quality the other way -- more density of a land facet, more diversity of facets, the better. This tool bridges the two by taking the numeric reciprocal of every cell: each output value is 1 divided by (the input value plus a small constant). Ground where density or diversity is high comes out with low cost, and the result can be handed directly to CorridorDesigner or Cost Distance as a resistance surface.
The dialog follows the input's shape. Give the tool a single-band raster -- a Diversity Indices surface, or one band of a density raster -- and it asks for a plain output raster name, exactly like the original ArcMap tool. Give it a multi-band raster -- this suite's own Land Facet Density raster -- and it instead asks for an output workspace and a name prefix, then writes one single-band cost raster per band in a single run, each named from the facet recorded in the density raster's metadata (for example "Inv_Valley_Cluster_2"). The parameters that do not apply to the current input are disabled. A multi-band inverted raster is never produced, because the least-cost tools these surfaces feed expect a single band.
The constant. Dividing by a cell whose value is exactly zero is undefined, and such cells would become NoData holes in the cost surface -- holes that least-cost analysis treats as impassable. Adding a small constant to every cell before inverting removes the problem, and the Land Facet manual strongly recommends it, suggesting 0.1 (which makes the diversity resistance formula exactly 1/(H' + 0.1), as published). The default here is 0.1. Clear the constant only for a deliberate reason; the tool will warn, and any zero cells then become NoData just as the original did. The constant also caps the maximum cost: with c = 0.1 the worst possible cell (value 0) costs 10 and the best possible density cell (proportion 1.0) costs about 0.91, an 11-to-1 range.
The linear method: ArcMap CorridorModel compatibility. The reciprocal is not the only way to turn suitability into cost. The original ArcMap CorridorDesigner CorridorModel tool converted a 0-100 habitat suitability model to cost internally as the linear complement -- cost = 100 - suitability, with a resulting cost of exactly 0 (perfect habitat) bumped to 1 so travel is never free -- and this tool's "Linear: 100 - x" method reproduces that conversion exactly, so corridors built in ArcGIS Pro can be made comparable with corridors built by the ArcMap tool from the same HSM. The two methods encode different ecological assumptions, and their corridors can take visibly different routes: the reciprocal punishes very poor habitat far more steeply -- under the linear rule, near-worthless habitat (suitability 1) costs about ten times what excellent habitat (suitability 90) costs, but under the reciprocal with c = 0.1 it costs about eighty times as much -- so reciprocal-based corridors avoid bad ground at almost any price, while linear-based corridors are more willing to shortcut through it when the detour is long. Neither is wrong; pick the assumption that matches how strongly your species avoids poor habitat. The linear method expects a 0-100 suitability surface: values above 100 would produce negative (invalid) costs and values that never exceed 1 produce a nearly flat surface, and the tool warns in both cases. The constant does not apply to the linear method and is disabled when it is selected. For density, diversity, and other proportion or index surfaces, use the reciprocal.
What the original was for, and what this one adds. In the published workflow the Invert Raster tool exists to invert the Shannon's Index (diversity) raster into the cost surface for the facet-interspersion corridor; the individual facet corridors get their cost surfaces from the Mahalanobis tool instead, which already produces low-is-good values. This version serves that same purpose -- run it on a Diversity Indices output -- and adds direct support for the Land Facet Density raster, for building corridors that simply follow each facet's abundance.
Do not invert a Mahalanobis distance raster. A Land Facet Mahalanobis output (D or D2) is already a valid cost surface exactly as written: low values mean close to the facet's typical, multivariate-ideal conditions, which is precisely the "cheap to cross" sense a corridor needs. Running this tool on one reverses that meaning -- the least typical, worst ground would become the cheapest to cross -- so if the input carries a Mahalanobis linkage record with D or D2 output, the tool warns loudly and explains why; feed the Mahalanobis raster to Least-Cost Corridor directly instead. The one Mahalanobis output type this does apply to is the p-value (typicality) raster, where -- like density -- high values mean good and the same inversion logic used for density and diversity is the right transform.
Stored density values are converted back to proportions first. Land Facet Density rasters store their 0-1 proportions as integers scaled by 10,000. Adding 0.1 to a raw stored value of, say, 6923 would make the constant meaningless and the cost curve unrecognizable. Whenever the input carries a density record -- the whole raster, or one of its bands given as "dens.tif\Band_3" -- values are converted back to true proportions before the constant is added, reproducing the published curve exactly; the run messages report the conversion. Values above the stored maximum (possible when a geodatabase has dropped the NoData declaration on a multi-band raster) are treated as NoData with a warning.
Every output knows its place in the chain. Each inverted raster is stamped with a machine-readable record in its metadata (the same Supplemental Information mechanism the other Land Facet tools use) stating what it was inverted from, which facet's band (when the source was a density raster), the constant used, whether the stored scaling was undone, and the analysis identifier carried through from the source -- so later steps, and a reader six months from now, can trace exactly how the cost surface was made.
Negative values. The reciprocal of a negative number is negative, and least-cost tools reject negative costs. Density and diversity surfaces are never negative, so this cannot arise from this tool family's own outputs -- but this tool will invert any raster, so if cells are still negative after the constant is added their inverted values are written as-is, faithfully to the original, and the tool warns with a count. If you see that warning, either the input is not a quality surface or the constant needs to be larger.
NoData. Input NoData stays NoData in the output. Cells that become NoData through division by zero are counted and reported separately, so you can tell missing input from a zero-valued one.
References. Land Facet Corridor Designer: Beier, P., and B. Brost. 2010, "Use of land facets to plan for climate change: conserving the arenas, not the actors," Conservation Biology 24:701-710 (https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1523-1739.2010.01422.x); Brost, B.M., and P. Beier. 2012, "Use of land facets to design linkages for climate change," Ecological Applications 22:87-103 (https://doi.org/10.1890/11-0213.1); Jenness, J., B. Brost, and P. Beier. 2013, "Land Facet Corridor Designer: Extension for ArcGIS," Jenness Enterprises (http://www.jennessent.com/arcgis/land_facets.htm). Corridor Designer tools: Majka, D., J. Jenness, and P. Beier. 2007, "CorridorDesigner: ArcGIS tools for designing and evaluating corridors" (http://corridordesign.org).

dialogReference.para: The raster to invert: a surface in which high values mean good habitat. A single-band input (a Diversity Indices / Shannon's Index raster, or one band of a density raster given as "dens.tif\Band_3") produces one output raster; a multi-band Land Facet Density raster produces one single-band cost raster per facet. When the input carries a density record its stored integer values are converted back to 0-1 proportions before the constant is added, and each facet is named in the messages and output metadata.

The output least-cost raster, used when the input is single band (the parameter is disabled otherwise). A name is suggested from the input. A folder path typed without an extension is written as a GeoTIFF.

Where the inverted rasters are written when the input is multi-band (the parameter is disabled otherwise) -- a folder or a geodatabase. One single-band cost raster is written per band; a folder destination produces GeoTIFFs.

The leading part of each output name in the multi-band case; the facet label from the density raster's records follows ("Inv_Valley_Cluster_2"), or the input name and band number when there is no record. Defaults to "Inv".
Reciprocal (the default): each cell becomes 1/(x + c) -- the Land Facet original, right for density, diversity, and other proportion or index surfaces, and strongly punishing of poor habitat.

Linear: each cell becomes 100 - x, the exact suitability-to-cost conversion the ArcMap CorridorDesigner CorridorModel tool applied internally to a 0-100 habitat suitability model (a resulting cost of exactly 0 is set to 1, as that tool did) -- choose it for ArcMap-comparable corridors from an HSM.
The two encode different assumptions about how costly poor habitat is; see the tool help.

A small constant added to every cell before taking the reciprocal, preventing zero cells from dividing to NoData and capping the maximum cost. The default 0.1 is the Land Facet manual's strong recommendation and reproduces the published diversity resistance formula 1/(H' + 0.1). Clear it only deliberately; zero-valued cells then become NoData, and the tool warns. Applies to the Reciprocal method only (disabled for Linear).

Optionally restrict a multi-band run. When the input is a Land Facet Density raster the list offers each facet by identifier and label; for other multi-band rasters supply plain band numbers. Leave empty to invert every band, which is the normal choice.

scriptExample.title: Invert Raster example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: A whole density raster (one cost surface per facet, into a workspace), then the diversity corridor's cost surface (single band, plain output path), then a habitat suitability model inverted with the linear ArcMap-CorridorModel rule. Pass None for the constant to add nothing (zero cells then become NoData).
scriptExample.code:
import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your installed path is shown in this tool's run messages
# Multi-band density -> one inverted cost raster per facet arcpy.jenness.InvertRaster( "landfacets_Density.tif", None, r"C:\project\cost", "Inv", "Reciprocal: 1 / (x + c)", 0.1)
# The diversity corridor's cost surface: 1 / (H' + 0.1) arcpy.jenness.InvertRaster( "facets_EffNum_q1.tif", r"C:\project\cost\Inv_Diversity.tif", None, "Inv", "Reciprocal: 1 / (x + c)", 0.1)
# A 0-100 HSM -> cost via the ArcMap CorridorModel rule (100 - x) arcpy.jenness.InvertRaster( "Black_Bear_HSI.tif", r"C:\project\cost\Inv_Black_Bear_lin.tif", None, "Inv", "Linear: 100 - x (ArcMap CorridorModel, for 0-100 HSMs)", None)
